title: Risk-Based Security Controls
metaDescription: Cybersecurity controls scoped to a facility's actual risk and consequence profile — not a generic checklist applied uniformly across dissimilar systems.
heroDek: A checklist treats every system the same. A control set built on consequence does not — it spends the most effort where a compromise would matter the most.
contextHeading: A control that costs the same everywhere shouldn't be applied everywhere
contextParagraphs: Generic control frameworks are written to apply broadly, which means applied uniformly they either overprotect low-consequence systems at real operational cost or underprotect high-consequence ones because the framework had no way to know which was which. Neither outcome is defensible when a regulator, or an incident, asks why a given control was or wasn't there.

GSS starts from consequence rather than from the framework. A system whose compromise could affect safety, security, or continuity of a protected function gets a materially different control set than a system whose compromise would be an inconvenience — and that distinction is documented, not assumed.

The result is a control set that is defensible on its own terms: every control on the list traces to a specific risk it addresses, and every risk of consequence has a control addressing it. That traceability is what a regulator, an auditor, or a new security director needs to see, and it is what a checklist alone cannot produce.

methodology.label: System Categorization
methodology.body: Systems grouped by the consequence of compromise, not by network location or vendor.

methodology.label: Threat & Risk Analysis
methodology.body: Realistic threat scenarios evaluated against each system category.

methodology.label: Control Selection
methodology.body: Controls chosen and tailored to the specific risk and consequence identified, not applied uniformly.

methodology.label: Gap Analysis
methodology.body: Existing controls compared against the target set, with gaps prioritized by consequence.

methodology.label: Implementation Support
methodology.body: Control deployment sequenced to close the highest-consequence gaps first.

methodology.label: Documentation
methodology.body: The rationale behind every control captured for audit, licensing, and regulatory review.

faq.q: Does a risk-based approach mean fewer controls than a checklist framework?
faq.a: Not necessarily fewer — better targeted. Some systems end up with more stringent controls than a generic framework would require; others legitimately need less.

faq.q: How are legacy OT systems handled, if they can't support modern controls?
faq.a: Compensating controls are identified and documented against the specific risk the legacy system presents, rather than left as an unaddressed gap.

faq.q: Does this replace a required regulatory framework, or work alongside it?
faq.a: Alongside it. The control set is built to satisfy the applicable regulatory baseline and then tailored further by consequence, not built as a substitute for it.
